findings.what: Derived-directory creation still has a pre-pin symlink race.
findings.why: _prepare_search_root checks .anomaly by pathname and then calls Path.mkdir(exist_ok=True); it repeats the same check/mkdir sequence for search. A shared-case mutator can replace .anomaly with a symlink after the check, causing search_root.mkdir at line 647 to create an outside search directory before _pin_search_root notices the rebind. This is a reachable path-escape write under the task's explicit concurrent/symlink-swap threat model and blocks AC2 containment. Create and open both components relative to a pinned case-root descriptor with mkdirat/openat-style dir_fd operations and O_NOFOLLOW rather than prechecking mutable pathnames.

findings.what: The derived-containment tests do not exercise the pre-pin directory-creation race.
findings.why: The existing swap test calls the real _prepare_search_root to completion and only then replaces search, while the pre-existing-symlink test is static. An implementation that follows a newly swapped .anomaly symlink during either mkdir therefore remains green. AC2's outside-write boundary is consumer-observable and security-sensitive, so add a deterministic Event-scheduled swap between validation and creation and assert that the outside sentinel and directory entries remain unchanged.

findings.what: No behavioral test distinguishes the private-copy repair from the previously green mutable-pathname reopen.
findings.why: Checkpoint 801f0e1 passed the full gate and the same 31 signal-search tests while DuckDB still reopened the verified case artifact through a mutable pathname; the bonus repair changed only production code. The current concurrency test pauses after verified_projection has already opened its connection, so reverting _open_private_projection to the vulnerable pathname flow would still pass. AC2/AC6 need an event-scheduled public-search case that ABA-swaps signals.duckdb after descriptor-based verification but around DuckDB open and proves the search returns the verified rows or fails closed, never rows from the replacement.

findings.what: The new private temporary projection lifecycle has no observable cleanup regression test.
findings.why: The implementation currently owns cleanup correctly, but the test file never observes temporary projection lifetime; removing _PrivateProjection's retained TemporaryDirectory or its cleanup call would leave all 31 tests green while leaking redacted projection files and directories. Add an isolated, parallel-safe lifecycle case that proves no private projection artifact remains after both a successful search and a query failure, without asserting private call shapes.

findings.what: The projection implementation still exceeds the maintainability boundary and combines unrelated responsibilities.
findings.why: The final module is 824 lines and owns temporary resource lifetime, descriptor/path containment, manifest verification, canonical parsing, provenance and metadata policy, public mapping, DuckDB persistence, and staging. This remains six-month maintenance debt under the authoritative less-than-200-line module directive, but it is not by itself a reachable correctness, security, data-loss, or acceptance failure.

findings.what: The public API still claims an atomic rebuild although the two artifacts are published separately.
findings.why: build_projection performs independent os.replace calls for signals.duckdb and signals-manifest.json. Failure after the database replacement can leave a new database paired with the old manifest. Verification fails closed and a later explicit rebuild can recover without canonical data loss, so this degenerate-filesystem edge is follow-up debt; remove the inaccurate atomicity claim or publish one generation through a single atomic indirection.
